recipe.history:
Char siu — Chinese BBQ pork — is one of the great roasted meat traditions of Cantonese cuisine, with roots tracing back to the roasting techniques documented in the Zhou dynasty texts of ancient China, where the slow fire-roasting of meats was considered a high culinary art. The name char siu (叉燒) means "fork roasted," a reference to the long forks used to hold strips of pork over open flames in traditional Cantonese kitchens. The marinade — soy sauce, hoisin, honey, five-spice, fermented red bean curd for color — is a study in balance: sweet, salty, savory, umami, and fragrant with anise and cinnamon and clove. Char siu arrived in America with Cantonese immigrant laborers in the mid-nineteenth century, first feeding railroad workers and mining communities, then becoming the beloved centerpiece of Chinatown barbecue shops from San Francisco to New York, where whole roasted pork strips hung in window displays became one of the most iconic sights in American urban food culture.

The American mall food court is a phenomenon that deserves its own culinary history. From the late 1970s through the 2000s, the food court was the most democratic dining space in America: a place where Chinese American takeout, Sbarro pizza, Subway sandwiches, Panda Express, Auntie Anne's pretzels, and Orange Julius existed in a kind of cheerful egalitarian proximity that no single restaurant could replicate. Char siu pork from a Chinatown-style vendor in a food court — or the approximation of it from chains like Panda Express — introduced Chinese-American flavors to suburban Americans who might not otherwise encounter them. The pretzel bun, another food court icon from the soft pretzel tradition of Auntie Anne's and Wetzel's Pretzels, brings its malty, slightly bitter, sodium-crusted character to this burger as a tribute to mall food culture's genius for putting unexpected things next to each other and having them work.

I spent significant portions of my adolescence in malls. Not shopping — mostly wandering, mostly eating. I know the smell of a food court in the afternoon, that particular combination of frying oil and sweet teriyaki glaze and yeast from the pretzel stand, with the cold mall air-conditioning underneath everything. I have eaten char siu rice plates and soft pretzels and slices of pizza in that smell hundreds of times, and I remember them with genuine affection: not as great cuisine, but as something honest and satisfying and specific to that time and place. This burger is a reconstruction of that memory, the way food sometimes can be — a pretzel bun carrying the salt and malt of the pretzel stand, char siu pork on top of a beef patty the way Panda Express sat next to the burger place, hoisin aioli connecting them the way the food court connected everything.

The medium rare standard holds even here, in a burger built from nostalgia and food court memory. The beef patty — the foundation of the whole construction — must reach 130–135°F (54–57°C) and no more. The char siu pork, glazed and caramelized on its exterior, provides sweetness and smoke on top; the hoisin aioli provides umami and fat; the pretzel bun provides crunch and salt. What holds all of this together is a medium rare patty with its pink, yielding interior acting as the soft counterweight to all that intensity above it. Well done would make the whole burger clench, turn sweet and dry and overwhelming. Medium rare keeps it open.
ingredients: Coarse sea salt or pretzel salt
600g pork tenderloin or pork shoulder, cut into 4cm-thick strips
1 tbsp fermented red bean curd (nam yue), mashed (or 1 extra tbsp hoisin)
900g freshly ground beef (80% chuck, 20% brisket blend)
6 slices provolone or mild Swiss cheese
instructions: 1. Marinate the char siu pork (at least 4 hours or overnight): Combine hoisin sauce, soy sauce, honey, Shaoxing rice wine, fermented red bean curd, five-spice, sesame oil, grated garlic, and grated ginger in a bowl. Add pork strips and toss to coat completely. Cover and refrigerate for at least 4 hours.

2. Roast the char siu: Preheat oven to 220°C (425°F) with a rack set over a foil-lined baking tray. Remove pork from marinade, reserving the marinade. Lay pork strips on the rack and roast for 20 minutes. Brush generously with reserved marinade, then roast for a further 10 minutes until the exterior is deeply caramelized and slightly charred at the edges. Rest for 10 minutes, then slice thinly against the grain.

3. Make the quick-pickled cucumber: Combine rice wine vinegar, sugar, kosher salt, and sesame oil in a small bowl and stir until dissolved. Add cucumber slices, toss, and refrigerate for at least 30 minutes.

4. Make the hoisin aioli: Whisk egg yolks and Dijon together until pale. Add neutral oil drop by drop while whisking until the emulsion establishes, then add the rest in a thin stream. Fold in hoisin sauce, rice vinegar, and grated garlic. Season with salt. Refrigerate until needed.

5. Make the pretzel buns: Combine bread flour, instant yeast, salt, and sugar in a stand mixer with a dough hook. Add softened butter and warm water, and mix on low for 2 minutes. Knead on medium-high for 8–10 minutes until the dough is smooth and slightly stiff. Place in an oiled bowl, cover, and rise for 1 hour until doubled.
6. Divide dough into 6 equal portions of about 130g. Shape into tight balls. Place on a parchment-lined baking sheet and rest uncovered for 20 minutes.

7. Preheat oven to 220°C (425°F). Bring 2 litres of water to a boil in a large pot. Add baking soda carefully (it will foam vigorously). Working in batches, submerge each dough ball in the baking soda bath for 30 seconds, turning once. Remove with a slotted spoon, drain briefly, and return to the parchment-lined sheet.

8. Brush each bun with beaten egg and sprinkle generously with coarse sea salt. Use a sharp knife or razor blade to score a cross or X on the top. Bake for 15–18 minutes until deep mahogany brown. Cool on a wire rack for at least 15 minutes.

9. Form the beef patties: Combine ground beef, soy sauce, sesame oil, garlic powder, salt, and pepper in a bowl. Mix gently just to distribute seasonings. Divide into 6 portions of 150g. Form into 10cm-wide, 2cm-thick patties with a thumb indent. Handle minimally.

10. Heat a cast-iron skillet with a thin film of neutral oil over high heat until smoking. Cook patties undisturbed for 3 minutes. Flip, place a slice of provolone on each patty, and cook for 2–2.5 more minutes. Confirm internal temperature of 130–135°F (54–57°C) for medium rare. Rest on a wire rack for 3 minutes.
11. Slice pretzel buns and toast cut-side down in a dry skillet over medium heat for 60 seconds — they are already richly flavored and need no butter.

12. Assemble each burger: Spread hoisin aioli on both cut faces of the bun. Place drained pickled cucumber slices on the bottom bun. Set the rested cheese-topped patty on top. Layer warm sliced char siu pork generously over the patty. Scatter sliced spring onions and toasted sesame seeds over the top. Cap with the top bun and serve immediately.
